landmarks.name: Robarts Library
facts: Its brutalist concrete tower is the main humanities and social sciences library, with more than 4.5 million books.
Construction began in 1968 and finished in 1973, at a cost of over $40 million. It is named for the 17th Premier of Ontario.

landmarks.name: Gerstein Science Information Centre
facts: It is the largest science and health science academic library in Canada.
It was the university's main library from 1892 to 1973, when the humanities collections moved to a new library on St. George Street.

landmarks.name: Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library
facts: It holds the university archives, including the papers of Margaret Atwood and Leonard Cohen.
In 2018 it acquired the oldest English-language book in Canada, a Cicero printed by William Caxton in 1481.

landmarks.name: E. J. Pratt Library
facts: It is Victoria College's library, named after a Canadian poet.
It was founded while the literary critic Northrop Frye was principal of Victoria College.

landmarks.name: John M. Kelly Library
facts: It is St. Michael's College's library, named after a former president of the college.

landmarks.name: Bora Laskin Law Library
facts: It is named after a former Chief Justice of Canada who once taught law at the university.

landmarks.name: Wetmore Hall
facts: It is one of the three halls of New College's serpentine residence.
It was first planned as a wing of New College for what became Innis College, which was founded separately in 1964.

landmarks.name: Wilson Hall
facts: It is one of the three halls of New College's serpentine residence, alongside Wetmore Hall and the New Building of 2003.

landmarks.name: Sir Daniel Wilson Residence
facts: It has six houses: Jeanneret, Taylor, Wallace, Hutton, Loudon and McCaul.
University College built it in 1954; its older neighbour, Whitney Hall, dates from 1931.

landmarks.name: Burwash Hall
facts: It is Victoria College's main residence, split into the Upper Houses and the Lower Houses.
Its Upper Houses were built in 1913 and its Lower Houses in 1931. It is named after Nathanael ____, president of Victoria from 1887 to 1912.

landmarks.name: Margaret Addison Hall
facts: It was built in 1959 to add women's residence rooms at Victoria College.

landmarks.name: Annesley Hall
facts: It is the oldest residence building at Victoria University.
Built in 1903 to a design by George Martel Miller, it was the first university residence built for women in Canada.

landmarks.name: Whitney Hall
facts: It is a University College residence named after a former Premier of Ontario.
The original hall was built in 1931, decades before its neighbour Sir Daniel Wilson Residence (1954).

landmarks.name: Morrison Hall
facts: It has five houses: Landsberg-Lewis, Perron, Wolfe, Bratty and Langley.
It was added in 2005 as University College's third residence.

landmarks.name: Graduate House
facts: It is a residence for master's and doctoral students, designed by Thom Mayne of Morphosis with Teeple Architects.
It opened on Harbord Street in 2000.

landmarks.name: Innis Residence
facts: It is a seven-storey apartment-style residence across the street from its college, at 111 St. George Street.
Built in 1994, it replaced the college's first residence, Vladimir House on Spadina Avenue.

landmarks.name: Woodsworth College Residence
facts: In 2001 the university began redeveloping the site to make room for it.

landmarks.name: Elmsley Hall
facts: A Ukrainian Catholic chapel, St. Sophia, is on its lower floor.
St. Michael's College built it in 1955 as a men's residence.

landmarks.name: St. Hilda's College
landmarks.wikipedia: St. Hilda's College, University of Toronto
facts: It is Trinity College's residence and is named after a 7th-century abbess of Whitby.
In 1903 it moved into a purpose-built building on the old Trinity College grounds in Trinity Bellwoods Park.

landmarks.name: Loretto College
facts: It is a women's residence of St. Michael's College.
Its college moved to St. George Street in 1937, and its residence here was built in 1958.

landmarks.name: Rowell Jackman Hall
facts: It is the newest of Victoria College's residence buildings, built in 1993.
Before it was built, the site held a parking lot and the historic Stephenson House.

landmarks.name: University College
facts: It was founded in 1853 as the non-denominational teaching arm of the University of Toronto.
Its main building, built from 1856 to 1859, was designed by Frederick William Cumberland and William George Storm.

landmarks.name: Trinity College
facts: It was founded in 1851 by Bishop John Strachan as an Anglican university.
After five decades as an independent institution, it joined the University of Toronto federation in 1904.

landmarks.name: Victoria College
facts: It began as Upper Canada Academy, founded in 1836 in Cobourg by the Wesleyan Methodists.
It federated with the University of Toronto in 1890 and moved from Cobourg to Toronto.

landmarks.name: Innis College
facts: It has its own cinema, the Town Hall, which hosts film festivals and free screenings.
Founded in 1964, it is named after the political economist Harold ____.

landmarks.name: Knox College
facts: It is a Presbyterian theological college in the Collegiate Gothic style.
Its building on the St. George campus was finished in 1915, designed by Chapman & McGiffin; the college itself was founded in 1844.

landmarks.name: Massey College
facts: It is a residential college for graduate students, designed by Canadian architect Ron Thom.
It opened in 1963 and admitted women only from 1974.

landmarks.name: Wycliffe College
facts: It is an evangelical Anglican seminary and a founding member of the Toronto School of Theology.
It was founded in 1877; its Dining Hall and Dormitory Wing were designed by Henry Bauld Gordon in 1907.

landmarks.name: Emmanuel College
facts: It is a theological college that appointed its first woman principal in 2018.
Its main building opened in 1931, the same year as Burwash Hall's Lower Houses, which were built for its theology students.

landmarks.name: Regis College
facts: It is the Jesuit school of theology in Canada.
It began in 1930 as a Jesuit philosophy college on Wellington Street and moved near its present site in 1976.

landmarks.name: Woodsworth College (Kruger Hall)
facts: Its college is named after the founder of the CCF party and began in 1974 to serve part-time students.

landmarks.name: Bahen Centre for Information Technology
facts: Its 8 floors hold about 50 labs, 10 lecture theatres and 300 offices, including computer science.
It opened in 2002; the entrance portico of a demolished house on the site is displayed in its lobby.

landmarks.name: Sidney Smith Hall
facts: It was completed in 1961 and is named after a former president of the university.

landmarks.name: Myhal Centre
facts: It is an engineering building that opened in 2018.

landmarks.name: Medical Sciences Building
facts: Its west wing is slated to be replaced by the planned Temerty Building.
The university has taught science on this site since about 1850; in 2025 the city designated the building under the Ontario Heritage Act.

landmarks.name: Lash Miller Chemical Laboratories
facts: It is the chemistry building, named after a chemistry professor at the university.

landmarks.name: McLennan Physical Laboratories
facts: An atmospheric observatory on the roof of its Burton Tower has measured stratospheric gases since 2001.

landmarks.name: Sandford Fleming Building
facts: It is named after the engineer who proposed worldwide standard time zones.
A fire in 1977 gutted much of the building.

landmarks.name: Galbraith Building
facts: It was built in 1960 to a design by Page & Steele Architects.

landmarks.name: Wallberg Building
facts: It was built in the late 1940s, when engineering classes moved back to Toronto after the war.

landmarks.name: Mechanical Engineering Building
facts: Camp labourers built it in the late 1940s from cement blocks instead of the campus's usual limestone.

landmarks.name: Lassonde Mining Building
facts: It opened in 1905 and is one of the oldest engineering buildings on campus.

landmarks.name: Ramsay Wright Building
facts: It is named after a 19th-century professor of natural history at the university.

landmarks.name: Leslie Dan Pharmacy Building
facts: Its faculty began in 1953, when the provincial college that trained pharmacists merged into the university.

landmarks.name: Rotman School of Management
facts: Its programs trace back to a commerce diploma first offered in 1901.

landmarks.name: Jackman Law Building
facts: It was designed by B+H Architects with Hariri Pontarini Architects.
It is named after Hal ____, whose $11 million gift in 2012 was the largest the faculty had ever received.

landmarks.name: Daniels Building (One Spadina)
facts: It houses the Faculty of Architecture, Landscape, and Design, on a crescent in the middle of a major avenue.
The Gothic Revival building, designed by James Avon Smith, was built in 1875 as the home of Knox College.

landmarks.name: Edward Johnson Building
facts: It is home to the Faculty of Music.

landmarks.name: OISE
landmarks.wikipedia: Ontario Institute for Studies in Education
facts: Its main complex stands at 252 Bloor Street West, above St. George subway station.
The complex was built from 1966 to 1969, designed by architect Kenneth Raymond Cooper; the institute was founded in 1965 by an act of the Ontario Legislature.

landmarks.name: Health Sciences Building
facts: It houses the Faculty of Nursing, established in 1933.

landmarks.name: Donnelly Centre
facts: It is a centre for cellular and biomolecular research, opened in 2005 and designed by Behnisch Architects.

landmarks.name: C. David Naylor Building
facts: It was called the Tanz Building until it was renamed in 2015.

landmarks.name: Jackman Humanities Building
facts: It used to be known as the Medical Arts Building.

landmarks.name: Northrop Frye Hall
facts: A bronze statue of the literary critic it is named after sits on a bench just west of it.

landmarks.name: Carr Hall
facts: Designed by Ernest Cormier and built in 1954, it is an example of the campus's early post-war architecture.

landmarks.name: Claude T. Bissell Building
facts: It houses the Faculty of Information and connects to the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library.
It is named after a former president of the University of Toronto.

landmarks.name: Schwartz Reisman Innovation Campus
facts: It is a two-tower innovation complex that houses the Vector Institute for Artificial Intelligence.
The Banting Institute was demolished in 2025 to make way for its second phase.

landmarks.name: Clara Benson Building
facts: It is named after one of the first women to earn a PhD at the university, in chemistry in 1903.

landmarks.name: Gerald Larkin Building
facts: It opened in 1962; the George Ignatieff Theatre was added to its northwest corner in 1979.

landmarks.name: Hart House
facts: Established in 1919, it is one of the earliest student centres in North America.
It was paid for by Vincent Massey and named after his grandfather, ____ Massey.

landmarks.name: Convocation Hall
facts: Al Gore gave a public lecture on climate change here in 2007.
Designed by Darling and Pearson, it was finished in 1907 at almost twice its estimated cost.

landmarks.name: Simcoe Hall
facts: It houses the offices of the university's president and Governing Council.
It was listed in the City of Toronto's Heritage Register in 1973.

landmarks.name: Soldiers' Tower
facts: It is a Gothic Revival bell and clock tower with a carillon of 51 bells.
Alumni raised $397,141 after the First World War to build it as a war memorial; it was designed by Henry Sproatt and Ernest Ross Rolph.

landmarks.name: Koffler Student Services Centre
facts: It houses the campus bookstore, the Career Centre and the health clinic.
It opened in 1909 as the Toronto Public Library's Central Reference Library, Ontario's largest Carnegie library.

landmarks.name: Student Commons
facts: The students' union moved its offices here, to 230 College Street, in 2021.

landmarks.name: Isabel Bader Theatre
facts: It is a Victoria College theatre that opened in March 2001.

landmarks.name: George Ignatieff Theatre
facts: It is Trinity College's theatre, named after a former provost.
It was added to the northwest corner of the Gerald Larkin Building in 1979; before that, Trinity's drama society performed at Hart House.

landmarks.name: Varsity Stadium
facts: It is home field for the university's football team.
Athletic events have been held on the site since 1898; the current stadium replaced the 1911 original in 2007.

landmarks.name: Varsity Arena
facts: It is the home rink of the university's ice hockey teams.
It opened on December 17, 1926, as one of the first arenas without pillars blocking the view from the seats.

landmarks.name: Goldring Centre
landmarks.wikipedia: Goldring Centre for High Performance Sport
facts: It is home to the Varsity Blues basketball and volleyball teams.
It was completed in 2014 at a cost of $58 million, designed by Patkau Architects with MacLennan Jaunkalns Miller.
